sources.title: Human History Map, imported civilization index
sources.note: Repository index checked directly: monte-alban is a circa state record from 323 BCE to 800 CE. This imported timing is compared with archaeological chronology rather than treated as an exact reign.

sources.title: Human History Map, representative Monte Albán border snapshot
sources.note: Local decoding of all twelve snapshots found the same 12-vertex regional polygon in every interval from 323 BCE to 800 CE, bbox -99.212,16.220 to -95.432,18.057. Monte Albán, Oaxaca, Mitla and Huajuapan test inside; Tehuantepec, Puerto Escondido and Puebla test outside. It is not a surveyed city or state frontier.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Historic Centre of Oaxaca and Archaeological Site of Monte Albán
sources.note: Official property synthesis checked for 500 BCE to about 850 CE chronology, terraces, dams, canals, pyramids, 300-metre esplanade, writing, planning, influence, later fortified phase, preservation and the explicit statement that the reason for eventual abandonment is not established.

sources.title: University of Michigan, Archaeological Research in Oaxaca: Origins of the State
sources.note: University research synthesis checked for early settlement, population estimates, defensive wall, conflict evidence, satellite communities and formation of one of Mexico’s earliest states. Presumptions about responsibility for individual attacks remain attributed to the research model.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum of Art, Monte Albán
sources.note: Institutional art-history essay checked for 500 BCE foundation, early population, plaza growth, tombs, the “1 Earthquake” calendrical glyph at San José Mogote and evidence of a Zapotec neighbourhood at Teotihuacan. Its peaceful-relations interpretation is presented beside a differing INAH interpretation.

sources.title: Instituto Nacional de Antropología e Historia, Monte Albán archaeological guide
sources.note: Official two-page guide checked for 500 BCE to 850 CE range, architecture and house classes, family tombs, Stelae 12 and 13, ruler 13 Owl, a female ruler on VG-2, Atzompa, Teotihuacan relations and the later reuse of Tomb 7.

sources.title: INAH Lugares, Monte Albán archaeological zone
sources.note: Official site guide checked for tribute, exchange, pottery, ball courts, elite residences, glyph-bearing monuments, incomplete decipherment and continued offerings after political collapse. Interpretations are kept distinct from directly observed structures.

sources.title: Feinman and Nicholas, The Foundation of Monte Albán, Intensification, and Growth
sources.note: Peer-reviewed synthesis checked for maize, beans and squash; the mountaintop’s poor access to prime farmland; household water and erosion work; linked rural growth; and the expansion of specialist pottery production for exchange.

sources.title: Ancient Mesoamerica, childhood and status in two Monte Albán households
sources.note: Peer-reviewed household study checked for two middle/high-status Classic-period domestic units, age-differentiated burial locations, inequality and the explicit caution that these households do not represent every child or family.

sources.title: INAH, Monte Albán Site Museum
sources.note: Official museum guide checked for the 650-piece collection, early writing, trade and Teotihuacan-style finds, long texts not fully deciphered, and human remains showing trepanation, cranial shaping, dental modification and stone inlays.

sources.title: Arqueología Mexicana, Rainwater management at Monte Albán’s ball court
sources.note: 2025 archaeological account checked for rain capture, distribution, drains, flood prevention and the channel linking the Main Plaza and ball-court area. The card explicitly does not relabel storm drainage as sewerage or toilets.

sources.title: Latin American Antiquity, The Power of Monuments in Ruin in Ancient Oaxaca
sources.note: Peer-reviewed article checked for collapse of the Monte Albán polity and large-scale abandonment about 800 CE, later offerings in the Main Plaza and the continued power of the ruined sacred landscape.

sources.title: INAH Lugares, The tombs of Monte Albán
sources.note: Official interpretation checked for Monte Albán as a civic-administrative capital until about 800-850, 249 recorded tombs, and burials placed within household spaces including masonry tombs, cists, pits and repurposed domestic features.

sources.title: INAH Lugares, The Treasure of Tomb 7 at Monte Albán
sources.note: Official museum entry checked for Alfonso Caso’s 1932 discovery and the later Mixtec collection of gold, silver, turquoise, obsidian, greenstone, crystal, amber, shell, pearls and coral, demonstrating craftsmanship and exchange networks. It is explicitly separated from Classic Zapotec city life.

sources.title: Ticha, Juan de Córdova’s 1578 Arte en lengua zapoteca
sources.note: Scholarly digital edition checked at folio 9r for the alphabetic Colonial Zapotec form “Niça” meaning water. The card labels it as a later Latin-script sample rather than pretending it reproduces Monte Albán’s glyphs.

sources.title: National Institute of Indigenous Languages, Zapotec language, 2026
sources.note: Official current language profile checked for Zapotec as one of Mexico’s Indigenous language groupings, its historical region, 62 recognized varieties and community-led writing-standardization work. Used to document continuity without equating all speakers with ancient Monte Albán.

proposedOverrides.summary: Monte Albán from mountaintop state formation through urban engineering, writing, family life, medicine and rainwater drains to political fragmentation and living Zapotec continuity.

batchIdentityNotes.decision: Ancient city and state centred on Monte Albán, not a synonym for all Zapotec peoples and not the later Mixtec reuse of the site. Indexed circa 323 BCE to 800 CE, although institutional archaeological sources place foundation around 500 BCE and political decline around 800-850 CE. Twelve intervals from world-bc323.json through world-700.json repeat one identical 12-vertex polygon, bbox -99.212,16.220 to -95.432,18.057. The outline contains Monte Albán, Oaxaca, Mitla and Huajuapan but excludes Tehuantepec, Puerto Escondido and Puebla; it is a coarse regional illustration, not a surveyed city boundary or proven frontier. Political collapse, site reuse and living Zapotec continuity are distinguished.
